connections.feedback: Without evidence or review, an error or missed theme travels straight to the team.
A fixed request keeps results consistent, quoted evidence makes the summary checkable, and a person closes the loop. Together these make the routine dependable.
A new request each week makes results uneven, and trusting the output removes the check.
A past good week does not guarantee this week's input will behave the same. Keep the check.

origin.author: READY builder
origin.source_reference: Original draft material; not an official assessment; awaiting owner review

connections.feedback: Reading for sense will not catch a wrong sum or an altered claim. Match the check to the kind of output instead.
Each kind of output fails differently: calculations slip, summaries drift, sources can be invented. The check should fit the failure.
Sources can be fake, but the calculation and summary can be wrong too.
A tool reviewing itself may repeat its errors. Use independent checks.

origin.author: READY builder
origin.source_reference: Original draft material; not an official assessment; awaiting owner review

connections.feedback: Reading for sense cannot find a wrong figure or a missing source. Recalculate, compare and open the sources instead.
Sampling saves time and may be fine for large volumes of low-risk text. For a small report where a single wrong figure matters, checking every item is safer.
connections.notes: Ambiguous: efficient, but a small report can be checked in full.

connections.feedback: The same tool is not an independent reviewer, because it can repeat its own errors. Use a calculator, the original text and the sources.
Use the check that suits each output: recalculate figures, compare summaries with the article, and confirm every source exists.

origin.author: READY builder
origin.source_reference: Original draft material; not an official assessment; awaiting owner review

connections.feedback: A note about AI does not tell the reader which parts to trust, and it moves your duty onto them.
Time pressure is when errors slip through. Past success does not remove the need to check key claims.
Full verification is ideal, but a flat refusal can be unhelpful when a partial, clearly labeled draft would meet the need. Some situations do call for refusing.
connections.notes: Ambiguous: depends on the stakes of the document.

connections.feedback: You can be honest about what is verified and prioritize the claims that matter most. The reader can then decide how to use it.

connections.feedback: Names add risk and are not needed to find themes in comments. Remove them and keep only the comment text.
Entering everything at once multiplies exposure if something is wrong. Begin with a small cleaned sample.
Stripping identifiers, starting small and using an approved tool keeps most of the value while limiting exposure.
Value and privacy can often both be protected with sensible steps, so a full refusal gives up too much.

origin.author: READY builder
origin.source_reference: Original draft material; not an official assessment; awaiting owner review

connections.feedback: Keeping a person involved is good practice, but this answer does not say how fairness will be checked. A concrete test adds more.
connections.notes: Ambiguous: right idea, not a method.

connections.feedback: Bias is often subtle and hard to see on a first read. Test the rubric on varied sample work to see how it treats different students.
The tool cannot reliably audit its own fairness, and it may simply say yes. Test the rubric on varied sample work instead.
Fairness shows up in results. Testing a range of sample work reveals criteria that favor one style of writing or background.

origin.author: READY builder

connections.feedback: A small success on typical cases does not show how it behaves on others. Test unusual and difficult examples before relying on it.
Past good results are not a guarantee on new, different cases. Test unusual examples and keep the checks that matter.
Ten typical cases may hide failures that appear with unusual input. Find where it breaks before relying on it.
Repeating the same cases only confirms what you already saw. Try unusual and difficult examples to find where it fails.

connections.feedback: A written routine helps, but handing someone a document rarely changes a habit by itself. It works best alongside a worked example.
connections.notes: Ambiguous: useful support, weak as a sole step.

connections.feedback: Public correction risks shame and defensiveness. Coaching works better in private.
A ban removes a useful tool without teaching the habit they lack. Helping them find a real error teaches more.
Finding a real error together makes the risk concrete, and agreeing a simple check gives them something to do next.

connections.feedback: Formatting is a task AI can do. The part that should stay human is the decision about priorities, not the layout.
Deciding priorities and accepting their consequences is a human job. AI can prepare information, but people choose.
Arithmetic can be done by AI (and checked), so it does not have to stay with people.
A person should read the proposals that matter, but AI summaries are a fair way to prepare. Whether it must stay human depends on how much weight the summaries carry.
connections.notes: Ambiguous: AI can help, but over-reliance on summaries affects the decision.

connections.feedback: A shorter request may stop step three being skipped, but deleting the other four steps gives up most of your task. Splitting the job into stages keeps all of it.
Another tool may skip steps too. Change how you ask first, for example by working one step at a time.
Long requests make it easy for steps to be dropped. Working one step at a time lets you confirm each before moving on.
Typing in capitals does not make the tool follow a request more closely. Break the job into steps instead.

connections.feedback: Hiding AI use undermines trust and may breach workplace rules. A guide should say when and how to be open about it.
People need a clear line on what may not be entered and which tools are allowed.
A good request reduces some errors but never guarantees correctness. A guide should say that output must still be checked.
Naming what must be checked, and who owns that check, makes accountability clear and gives people a rule to follow.

origin.author: READY builder

connections.feedback: A checking rule gives learners a habit they can follow every time, which matters more than any single tip.
Hiding use makes it harder to learn from mistakes and to build trust. Learners do better when use is open and discussed.
No request makes output always correct. Good wording helps, but checking is still needed, and a guide should say so.
Clear limits on information and tools give new users a safe place to start.

connections.feedback: A small success on typical cases does not show how it behaves on others.
Repeating the same cases only confirms what you already saw.
Ten typical examples may hide failures on unusual work. Find where the helper breaks before relying on it, and decide what checks remain.
A tool's stated confidence is not a measure of accuracy. It can sound highly confident when it is wrong.

connections.feedback: An approved tool is part of a safe setup, and some workplaces require it. But approval alone does not limit what you put in, so many experts would also remove the identifiers.
connections.notes: Ambiguous: necessary in many workplaces, but not sufficient alone.

connections.feedback: Entering the whole batch with names multiplies the exposure if something goes wrong. Clean first and start small.
Sorting by topic does not need names. Removing identifying details limits what could be exposed if something goes wrong.
A tool working well before says nothing about whether client details are safe in it. Limit what you enter.

connections.feedback: The tool does not keep a reliable record of your team's routine. Keep your own written version.
A written routine, with its checks and who owns them, survives people leaving and lets others run and fix it.
Once your colleague has left, nobody can ask them. Write the routine down while they are still here.
A routine that has worked can still fail when the person who understood it is gone. Document it.
